strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: addressing asynchronous policy staleness and communication latency in geographically distributed reinforcement learning for LLMs.
The intuition of replacing high-variance token-level importance sampling ratios with smoother sequence-level or expectation-based estimators is an interesting direction for stabilizing off-policy RL.
The paper is structured logically and includes detailed visual analyses of latency, KL divergence, and gradient variance dynamics.
weaknesses: Flawed sequence probability formulation: In Eq. (9), the sequence probabilities are defined as geometric means over token probabilities, i.e., $p(y|x) = (\prod_{t=1}^T p(y_t|x, y_{<t}))^{1/T}$. This is the geometric mean (perplexity-like measure), not a valid joint probability distribution over sequences. It does not integrate/sum to 1 over candidate sequences of length $T$, undermining the validity of subsequent importance sampling derivations.

Fundamental statistical bias in Group Expectation Importance Weighting: In Eq. (12) and Listing 1, the individual proposal likelihood $q(y|x)$ in the denominator is replaced by a prompt-group expectation $\hat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q(y|x)]$, which is identical for all samples $y_i$ generated for a given prompt $x$. As a result, the importance weight becomes proportional to $p(y|x)$ and completely ignores $q(y|x)$. Because $y \sim q$, this estimator does not target $\mathbb{E}_p[r(x,y)]$; instead, it weights samples by $p(y)q(y)$, introducing severe and uncharacterized estimation bias over high-dimensional sequence spaces where probabilities span many orders of magnitude.

Vacuous theoretical bounds in Theorem 1: The discrete space proof in Appendix A.1 relies on bounding $A = (\sum q_i^2)^2 \ge 1/n^2$, where $n$ is the cardinality of the discrete action/sequence space $\mathcal{X}$. For autoregressive generation over vocabulary size $V$ and length $T$, $n \approx V^T$ (e.g., $(10^5)^{1000}$). Consequently, the condition for variance reduction requires $D_{KL}(p \parallel q) > \log(n^2+1) \approx 2 T \log V$, which requires astronomical KL divergence (thousands to tens of thousands of nats). In contrast, the KL divergence in practical training (and in Figure 6a) is around $10^{-3}$ nats. Hence, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 provide no meaningful theoretical guarantee for language models.

Discrepancy between methodology and experimental implementation: Section 3.3 introduces defensive sampling (Eq. 15) to mitigate bias by blending with $p(y|x)$. However, Section 4.3 explicitly notes that 'None of the methods employed defensive sampling mechanisms,' and Listing 1 confirms that the actual code runs without defensive sampling. Presenting a theoretical mitigation that is not evaluated in the main empirical results is problematic.

Missing asynchronous RL baselines: The paper compares solely against GRPO and GSPO running under stale data. However, extensive prior literature addresses asynchronous and off-policy RL (e.g., IMPALA/V-trace, AREAL, AsyncFlow, LlamaRL, or standard off-policy clipping corrections). None of these established asynchronous RL techniques are compared against.

Narrow experimental evaluation: Experiments are conducted exclusively on a single model (Qwen3-1.7B) and a single task domain (MATH-500). Furthermore, while Section 4.2 presents a ZeroMQ-based wide-area communication framework, all reported experiments rely on simulated artificial delays rather than empirical WAN benchmarking.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and practically relevant problem: mitigating policy staleness and importance sampling instability in asynchronous, decentralized reinforcement learning for large language models.
The paper provides an end-to-end framework implementation (HeteroRL) including streaming communication, latency simulation, and sample-level weighting.
The empirical analysis exploring the relationship between communication delay, KL divergence, and gradient estimation error provides useful qualitative insights into asynchronous RL dynamics.
weaknesses: Fundamental flaw in the importance sampling formulation: Standard importance sampling relies on the identity $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}[(p(y)/q(y)) f(y)] = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p}[f(y)]$. In GEPO, replacing $q(y|x)$ in the denominator with a group-level expectation/constant $\hat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q(y|x)]$ means the expectation under the rollout policy $q$ becomes $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim q}[(p(y)/\hat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q]) f(y)] \propto \sum_y q(y) p(y) f(y)$. This does not estimate the policy gradient under $p$, but rather heavily biases optimization toward trajectories where $p(y)q(y)$ is high, breaking the core principle of off-policy correction.

Vacuous theoretical bounds: Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 state that $\text{Var}_{\text{std}} > \text{Var}_{\text{new}}$ holds when $D_{KL}(p \parallel q) > \log(n^2 + 1)$, where $n$ is the size of the discrete sample space $\mathcal{X}$. For autoregressive generation over a vocabulary $V$ and sequence length $T$, the sequence space size is $n = |V|^T$. Consequently, $\log(n^2 + 1) \approx 2T \log |V|$, which easily exceeds thousands or tens of thousands of nats. In practice, the observed KL divergences are on the order of $10^{-3}$ (as shown in Figure 6a). Therefore, the theoretical guarantee is completely vacuous in realistic LLM settings.

Questionable baseline tuning and collapse: In Table 2, both GRPO and GSPO collapse dramatically even in the zero-delay (synchronous online) setting (e.g., GRPO drops from 77.1 to 41.2; GSPO drops from 78.2 to 31.6). In standard online RL training of LLMs, standard GRPO does not collapse so catastrophically when properly tuned with appropriate learning rate, clipping, and KL penalties. This indicates that the baselines may have been poorly tuned, artificially amplifying the apparent stability advantage of GEPO.

Discrepancy between proposed method and experimental setup: Section 3.3 introduces defensive sampling with coefficient $\epsilon$ to mitigate estimator bias and smooth the denominator. However, Section 4.3 explicitly notes: 'None of the methods employed defensive sampling mechanisms', and Listing 1 confirms that only the raw group-expectation denominator was implemented. Introducing a core mechanism in the methodology only to omit it from the evaluation undermines the presentation and completeness of the work.

Limited empirical evaluation: The empirical evaluation is restricted to a single small model (Qwen3-1.7B) and a single dataset (MATH-500). There are no evaluations on other standard reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, OlympiadBench, code tasks), larger models, or comparisons against established asynchronous RL frameworks (e.g., AReal, LlamaRL, AsyncFlow).

strengths: Timely and practically important problem: Asynchronous, decoupled, and decentralized reinforcement learning is crucial for scaling LLM post-training across geographically distributed or heterogeneous compute clusters.
Comprehensive empirical analysis of the relationship between communication latency, policy staleness, KL divergence, and gradient/importance weight variance (Section 4.4, Figures 6 and 7).
Clear architectural description of the HeteroRL framework decoupling actor/sampler rollouts and parameter optimization, alongside the simulated delay modeling.
weaknesses: Theoretical flaws and vacuous bounds in Theorem 1: The paper claims that GEPO exponentially reduces importance weight variance when $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \parallel q) > \log(n^2 + 1)$ (Equation 41/43). For sequence generation with vocabulary size $|V|$ and sequence length $T$, the discrete state space cardinality is $n = |V|^T$. Consequently, $\log(n^2 + 1) \approx 2 T \log |V|$, which evaluates to tens of thousands. However, real-world KL divergences in LLM RL are typically on the order of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-1}$ (as plotted in Figure 6a, $\approx 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$). Hence, the lower bound $\exp(D_{\mathrm{KL}}) - (n^2 + 1)$ is an astronomically large negative number (e.g., $\approx -10^{1000}$), rendering Theorem 1 mathematically vacuous in explaining the empirical setting.

Methodological inconsistency and bias in Importance Sampling: Replacing the sample-specific behavior probability $q(y|x)$ with the within-group expectation $\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q(y|x)]$ in the denominator removes sample-specific density correction. In effect, the denominator becomes a constant scaling factor for the entire group, meaning gradients are scaled by $p(y|x)$ rather than correcting for off-policy sampling probability $q(y|x)$. Furthermore, while Section 3.3 introduces defensive sampling to counteract this bias, the authors state on page 10 that 'None of the methods employed defensive sampling mechanisms' in the experiments, leaving the core theoretical mitigation untested.

Severely degraded baseline performance in the synchronous setting (Delay 0): In Table 2, both GRPO and GSPO suffer severe collapse at Delay 0 (GRPO drops from 77.1% Best to 41.2% Last; GSPO drops from 78.2% Best to 31.6% Last). In standard online LLM RL setups with proper KL penalty and learning rates, GRPO does not exhibit this level of catastrophic collapse at zero delay. This strongly suggests suboptimal hyperparameter tuning (e.g., learning rate schedule, clipping parameters, or rollout batch sizes) for the baselines rather than an intrinsic failure mode addressed solely by GEPO.

Limited evaluation scope: Experiments are restricted to a single model (Qwen-1.7B) and a single benchmark (MATH-500). Evaluation across multiple model scales (e.g., 7B, 14B) and diverse reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K, OlympiadBench, Code/HumanEval) is necessary to substantiate generalizability.

Lack of real-world distributed validation: While Section 4.2 details a ZeroMQ-based wide-area network toolkit, the experimental results are conducted exclusively under a simulated log-normal delay environment. Validation on actual geographically distributed heterogeneous nodes is missing.

strengths: Timely and practically motivated problem: addressing policy staleness and importance weight variance in geographically distributed, asynchronous RL for LLM post-training is a crucial direction as training clusters become increasingly distributed.

Comprehensive system perspective: HeteroRL provides end-to-end design details for handling high-latency environments, including realistic latency distributions (up to 1800s), a ZeroMQ-based asynchronous toolkit, and localized reward computation to eliminate unnecessary communication barriers.

Promising empirical stability: across mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AMC2023, AIME2024, AIME2025, MATH500), GEPO demonstrates substantially improved stability and resistance to performance collapse under high policy staleness (delay=64) compared to GRPO and GSPO, alongside solid zero-delay performance.
weaknesses: Theoretical flaws and vacuous bounds in Theorem 1: The lower bound in Eq. (30) relies on $D_{KL}(p||q) > \log(n^2 + 1)$. For sequence generation where trajectories have length $T$, the discrete state space size is $n = |V|^T$, rendering $\log(n^2 + 1)$ astronomically large and the condition completely vacuous. Even if considered at the single-token level with vocabulary $|V| \approx 1.5 \times 10^5$, $\log(n^2 + 1) \approx 24$ nats, whereas typical per-token KL divergence in LLM RL training is around $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ nats. Additionally, Eq. (22) is attributed to Pinsker's inequality, whereas it is actually an application of Jensen's inequality relating KL divergence to chi-square divergence.

Unanalyzed estimator bias: Standard importance sampling divides by $q(y)$ specifically to ensure an unbiased gradient estimate of the target objective $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p}[A(x,y)]$. In GEPO, replacing $q(y)$ with a group-averaged scalar $\hat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q]$ removes the sequence-specific denominator, causing the expected update to be proportional to $\sum_y q(y) \nabla_\theta p(y) A(y)$. This fundamentally overweights actions favored by the behavior policy $q$ and changes the stationary points of optimization. The paper acknowledges GEPO is biased but provides no theoretical analysis, bounds, or convergence guarantees regarding this bias.

Missing comparisons with established variance-reduction / off-policy baselines: While replacing denominators with group averages trivially suppresses variance, standard off-policy RL literature provides several principled variance reduction techniques, such as self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), V-trace / truncated importance weights, and adaptive clipping. Comparing solely against GRPO/GSPO misses existing off-policy correction mechanisms tailored for asynchronous RL.

Lack of statistical significance reporting: The experimental results across benchmarks are reported as single-run point estimates without standard deviations or multiple random seeds, which is particularly critical in RL training where run-to-run variance and collapse can be stochastic.

strengths: Relevant and timely motivation: As LLM reasoning post-training scales, decoupling rollout generation from learner parameter updates to enable asynchronous, distributed, and geographically decentralized training across heterogeneous hardware is an important direction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on mathematical reasoning benchmarks: The authors evaluate on standard reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, AMC2023, AIME2024, AIME2025) comparing against multiple competitive baselines including GRPO, GSPO, BNPO, and Dr.GRPO under both online and delayed settings.

Useful system and engineering insights: The paper highlights practical engineering considerations for distributed RL, notably the localized reward computation which avoids cross-worker all-gather communication for group statistics.
weaknesses: Fundamental theoretical issue with the GEPO estimator: In standard importance sampling, dividing by $q(y|x)$ cancels the sampling distribution density, yielding an unbiased estimate of $\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p}[A(x,y)]$. By replacing $q(y|x)$ in the denominator with a group-averaged expectation $\hat{\mathbb{E}}_q[q(y|x)]$ (which is independent of the specific trajectory $y$), the resulting objective effectively optimizes $\sum_y p(y) q(y) A(x,y) / \mathbb{E}_q[q]$ rather than $\sum_y p(y) A(x,y)$. This is not merely a small finite-sample bias; it changes the objective to weight samples proportionally to $p(y)q(y)$, heavily suppressing low-probability paths and violating the policy gradient theorem even in the zero-delay online setting ($p=q$).

Flaws and uninformative bounds in Theorem 1 (Appendix A): (1) In Appendix A.1, Eq. (19) erroneously defines $I_2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{p_i^2}{q_i}$, which is identical to the formula for $I_1$ in Eq. (18), whereas the continuous counterpart indicates it should be $\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^2 q_i$. (2) The lower bound for variance reduction requires $D_{\text{KL}}(p \parallel q) > \log(n^2 + 1)$. For token sequences or large vocabulary sizes $n$, $\log(n^2 + 1)$ is on the order of tens or hundreds, whereas the empirical KL divergence reported in Figure 5a is on the order of $10^{-3}$. Hence, the theorem fails to provide guarantees in the operating regime of interest. (3) Comparing the variance of an unbiased estimator directly against the variance of a heavily biased estimator without analyzing mean squared error (MSE) is theoretically misleading, as a trivial constant estimator has zero variance.

Absence of system performance and throughput evaluation: HeteroRL is heavily framed as an asynchronous framework for heterogeneous hardware (e.g., NVIDIA and Ascend chips across WANs). However, the experimental results present only model task accuracy (Pass@1) under simulated step delays. Crucial distributed systems metrics—such as actual wall-clock speedup, throughput (tokens/second), network bandwidth consumption, and overhead comparisons between synchronous and asynchronous pipelines—are completely omitted.

Mathematical and notation inconsistencies: There is an inconsistency between the definition of the loss in Eq. (1) / Eq. (3), the gradient decomposition in Eq. (5), and the actual implementation in Listing 1. In Listing 1 line 7, `coef_1` scales by `learner_seq_p`, whereas Eq. (5) displays token-level derivatives $p'_{i,t}(\theta) / E_q q$ without explaining how sequence-level likelihoods and token gradients interact under clipping.

strengths: Practical and timely motivation: Decentralized and asynchronous reinforcement learning for LLMs across geographically distributed and heterogeneous hardware addresses a pressing engineering bottleneck in scaling post-training.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarks: The empirical evaluation covers multiple reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, AMC2023, AIME2024, AIME2025) using both 1.7B and 8B parameter models under various latency regimes.

Helpful systems insights: The paper identifies practical system bottlenecks in distributed RL, such as reward synchronization overhead, and proposes localized reward computation to eliminate cross-process all-gather operations.

Detailed analysis of training dynamics: The authors monitor several diagnostic quantities during training, including importance weight variance, gradient norms, and empirical correlations between delay steps and policy divergence.
weaknesses: Vacuous theoretical guarantee in Theorem 1: The condition for guaranteed variance reduction requires D_KL(p || q) > log(n^2 + 1), where n is the cardinality of the discrete sample space. For sequence generation over vocabulary V and sequence length T, n = |V|^T (e.g., ~150,000^2048), requiring D_KL to exceed tens of thousands of nats. In practice, training KL divergence is on the order of 10^-5 to 1 nat. Thus, the theoretical guarantee never applies to sequence-level LLM training, rendering the theorem practically vacuous.

Fundamental flaw and unaddressed bias in the GEPO estimator: Standard importance sampling requires weighting by p(y)/q(y) to ensure an unbiased gradient estimator: E_q[(p(y)/q(y)) 
abla \log p(y) A(y)] = 
abla E_p[A(y)]. By replacing q(y) with a group constant E_q[q], the resulting update is proportional to \sum_y p(y) q(y) 
abla \log p(y) A(y). This fundamentally distorts the optimization landscape by weighting gradients by the product distribution p(y)q(y) rather than correcting for policy mismatch. Reducing importance weight variance by replacing the individual denominator with a constant is trivial (e.g., setting weights to a constant yields zero variance), but severely impairs the estimator's consistency without any theoretical justification for policy convergence.

Conceptual misunderstanding of Monte Carlo integration in Equation (2): The authors state that for y^1, ..., y^G ~ q, using the sample mean (1/G) \sum q(y^i) 'would introduce bias due to ignoring relative sampling probabilities'. This is mathematically incorrect: because samples are drawn i.i.d. from q, the sample mean (1/G) \sum q(y^i) is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of E_q[q] = \int q(y)^2 dy. In contrast, the heuristic weighted estimator \sum q(y^i)^2 / \sum q(y^i) asymptotically converges to \int q(y)^3 dy / \int q(y)^2 dy, which is biased.

Unfair baseline configuration in online RL: The paper explicitly notes in Section 4.1 and B.1 that KL regularization was intentionally removed during online training to 'better evaluate inherent stability'. Standard GRPO relies on KL penalties or clipping to maintain policy stability; removing it naturally causes standard baselines to suffer reward collapse (e.g., GRPO dropping from 44.2 to 19.0 in Table 3). This setup artificially favors GEPO, whose denominator aggregation acts as an aggressive heuristic dampener.

Discrepancy between the heterogeneous distributed motivation and experimental execution: While the paper frames HeteroRL around distributed physical hardware across WANs (mixing Ascend and NVIDIA chips), the core experimental delay settings are implemented via a simulated delay queue with shared file paths (torch.save_pretrained to disk with artificial sleep times), leaving true multi-node WAN performance undemonstrated.
